chunks: "A LiPo is basically a thin sandwich: a cathode and an anode separated by a separator that is only some tens of microns thick, wetted with a flammable electrolyte, all in a soft foil pouch.
If you puncture it, the sharp object pushes through those layers and connects the electrodes, or the foil layers, directly.
That's an internal short circuit: the energy in the cell dumps through a tiny spot in the cell itself.
Because the short is localized and inside the cell, all the heat is released right there.
Tens of amps through a spot the size of a pinhead heats it very fast, melts the separator around it, and makes the short bigger.
That heat starts the exothermic breakdown reactions, so you get thermal runaway: venting of flammable gas, fire, toxic fumes.
The pouch has no rigid can, and air and moisture get in, which makes it worse. The scary part is that no electronics can help.
A protection circuit or fuse sits in the external path. The short is inside the cell, so it can't be interrupted.
And the damage may be partial and delayed: a pack that was only dented can ignite hours later. A lower state of charge reduces the severity, but it doesn't make it safe."
